titleEn: Create for me a pure heart
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: The confession psalm, headed by the one moment in David's life he would least want quoted, and then read for three thousand years by everyone else. Verse 17, the request that God open the speaker's lips, is said silently at the start of every Amidah, so most of this psalm's users meet it one line at a time without knowing where the line comes from. For a learner it is the best drill in the book for the imperative with an object suffix: wash me, purify me, create for me, restore to me, uphold me, deliver me. Count how many verbs end in the same two letters and the grammar teaches itself.

stichs.en: For the leader.
A psalm of David.

verses.summary: A performance note before a private confession. Whatever this was when it was said, it was filed as music for the choirmaster.

stichs.en: When Nathan the prophet came to him,
after he had gone in to Bath-sheba.

verses.summary: The superscription names the episode of 2 Samuel 11 and 12 and refuses to soften it. Note that the name Bath-sheba is two Hebrew words, the second the woman's own name.

stichs.en: Be gracious to me, God, according to Your kindness;
according to the abundance of Your mercies, wipe out my transgressions.

verses.summary: The measure asked for is not justice but the size of the other party's kindness. The verb translated wipe out is what you do to writing, not to a stain.

stichs.en: Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity,
and purify me from my sin.

verses.summary: Three different words for wrongdoing appear in two verses, and each takes its own verb of removal. The washing verb is the one used for laundering cloth.

stichs.en: For I myself know my transgressions,
and my sin is before me always.

verses.summary: The pronoun is redundant in Hebrew and therefore emphatic: nobody has to inform him. What follows is not a discovery but something he cannot get out of his field of vision.

stichs.en: Against You, You alone, have I sinned,
and what is evil in Your eyes I have done,
so that You are justified when You speak,
in the right when You judge.

verses.summary: The hardest line in the psalm, since there were two other people in the story. The claim is jurisdictional rather than moral: the verdict he is accepting is God's, and he concedes it in advance.

stichs.en: Behold, in iniquity I was brought forth,
and in sin did my mother conceive me.

verses.summary: The plea widens from an act to a condition. Whether this describes human nature or is the exaggeration of a man at his lowest is exactly what readers have argued about.

stichs.en: Behold, You desire truth in the hidden parts,
and in the closed place You make me know wisdom.

verses.summary: Both nouns for the inward place are rare and unclear, which is fitting. The turn is from what was done outside to what is wanted inside.

stichs.en: Purge me with hyssop and I shall be pure;
wash me and I shall be whiter than snow.

verses.summary: The vocabulary here is priestly, taken from ritual purification rather than from the law court. The speaker asks to be handled like an object that can be made fit for use again.

stichs.en: Make me hear joy and gladness;
let the bones You crushed rejoice.

verses.summary: Guilt is described as a physical injury, and the one who caused it is the one asked to undo it. Hearing comes before rejoicing: the news arrives first.

stichs.en: Hide Your face from my sins,
and wipe out all my iniquities.

verses.summary: Everywhere else in the psalms a hidden face is the disaster being complained about. Here it is the request, and only the sins are to be out of view.

stichs.en: Create for me a pure heart, God,
and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

verses.summary: The centre of the psalm and the point where cleaning stops being enough. The verb is the one used for the creation of the world, and in the Bible it never takes a human subject.

stichs.en: Do not cast me away from before You,
and do not take Your holy spirit from me.

verses.summary: The fear named is not punishment but dismissal. Saul is the model in the background: a king from whom the spirit departed and who was not told how to get it back.

stichs.en: Restore to me the joy of Your salvation,
and let a willing spirit uphold me.

verses.summary: Not the salvation itself, which he still has, but the joy of it, which he has lost. Third of three requests built on the word for spirit, after steadfast and holy.

stichs.en: Let me teach transgressors Your ways,
and sinners will return to You.

verses.summary: The first thing the repaired man offers to do is give the lesson away. This verse is the reason a private confession ended up in a public songbook.

stichs.en: Deliver me from bloodguilt, God, God of my deliverance;
let my tongue sing out Your righteousness.

verses.summary: The one word in the psalm that points at a specific crime rather than at sin in general. What the freed tongue is to sing is not the speaker's innocence but the judge's rightness.

stichs.en: My Lord, open my lips,
and my mouth will declare Your praise.

verses.summary: Said before every Amidah, standing, before a word of the prayer itself. The premise is that even the ability to ask has to be given first.

stichs.en: For You do not desire a sacrifice, or I would give it;
a burnt offering You do not accept.

verses.summary: He would pay if paying worked, and says so. The offering is refused not because it is too small but because it is the wrong currency.

stichs.en: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit;
a broken and crushed heart, God, You will not despise.

verses.summary: The line the whole psalm was walking toward, and the only altar it names. Breaking, which was the injury in verse 10, has become the offering.

stichs.en: Do good in Your favour to Zion;
build the walls of Jerusalem.

verses.summary: The voice goes from one man to a whole city in a single line. Broken walls answer a broken heart, and the same repair is asked for both.

stichs.en: Then You will desire sacrifices of righteousness, burnt offering and whole offering;
then they will offer up bulls upon Your altar.

verses.summary: The offerings refused three verses earlier are accepted here, and the word doing the work is then. Nothing about the altar has changed except the order of events.

pardes.body: Two verses of heading, then four movements. Verses 3 to 11 ask for the record to be erased and the man to be washed, in the vocabulary of laundry and ritual purity. Verses 12 to 14 stop asking for cleaning and ask for manufacture: {{12.2}}, create, and then renew and restore. Verses 15 to 19 turn outward, promise a lesson, and redefine what an offering is. Verses 20 and 21 leave the individual entirely for Zion and its walls. Those last two verses ask for a rebuilt city and working sacrifices right after the psalm has said that sacrifices are not what is wanted; many readers take them as a later addition made when the psalm entered communal use, and others read the whole thing as one composition that moves deliberately from the person to the nation. The question is disputed and the text gives no way to settle it.

The cleansing words are borrowed from the sanctuary. {{9.1}}, hyssop, is the plant used in the Torah to sprinkle the blood on the doorposts in Egypt, to purify a person healed of the skin affliction, and in the water of purification made with the red heifer. So the speaker is asking to be treated as a contaminated object handled by a priest, not as a defendant. Against that, {{12.2}} is a different register altogether: it is the verb of Genesis 1, and in biblical Hebrew only God is ever its subject, so what is asked for in verse 12 is not repair but a new thing. {{4.0}} is an imperative meaning make much, used adverbially, which is why English versions say thoroughly. {{16.1}} is literally bloods, plural, and it can mean bloodguilt or a violent death; which one David is asking to be spared is not decided by the grammar.

The tradition reads verse 15 as the answer to an obvious question: why is this in the book at all, and why with the heading naming Nathan and Bath-sheba. The reading is that the fall is recorded so that the repentance can be, and that a man who had not fallen could not have taught this. So the psalm is treated as the working manual for teshuvah rather than as one king's private business, which is why it belongs to the penitential material rather than to the historical books. Two of its lines were then lifted out and given jobs of their own: {{17.1}}, my lips, opens every Amidah, and verse 12 is sung on its own to more tunes than any other verse here. Read that way, the psalm answers Nathan's accusation not by defending anything but by making the accusation public property.

The mystical reading takes verse 19 literally as a theory of offerings: the altar receives what is broken, and a whole heart has nothing to put on it. Breaking is therefore not the damage that has to be repaired before service can start, it is the material of the service. {{19.4}}, heart, is described as both broken and crushed, two words for the same state, and the reading turns the crushing of verse 10 into the currency of verse 19. Alongside this runs the reading of verse 12 as creation from nothing performed inside a person: the old heart is not cleaned, it is replaced, and the request is possible only because the verb belongs to the one who made the world out of no prior thing. The two readings meet at the same place, which is that nothing usable survives the process except what is given back.
